title: How do you get a second opinion on your investment portfolio?
summary: Ask a fee-only planner, your brokerage or Astor to review what you own, and check how they’re paid and whether they owe you a fiduciary duty.
body_markdown:
### How much does a second opinion on a portfolio cost?


It depends on the route. Fee-only planner networks like XY Planning Network and Garrett Planning Network don’t publish a standard rate, because each planner sets its own, and Garrett planners estimate the fee at a free first meeting. Schwab says a conversation with its Financial Consultants is complimentary. Astor is free to start, and as of November 2026 Pro is $19 a month and Max is $29 a month, with lower prices billed yearly.


### Can I get a second opinion without moving my money?


Yes. A second opinion is a review, not a transfer. A planner works from your statements, and Astor connects to your existing accounts so it can see your holdings, but it can’t move money. Be cautious with anyone who makes moving your accounts a condition of reviewing them.


### Is a free portfolio review worth it?


Yes, often. A free review from your brokerage or an adviser can be thorough. Ask how the firm would be paid if you took its advice, and read its Form CRS, before you act on it.


### How often should I get a second opinion on my portfolio?


There’s no fixed schedule. Many people get one when something changes, like a new job, an inheritance, a position that grew far larger than planned or retirement getting closer. Between those moments, a yearly look at your own portfolio covers most of what a reviewer would check.


### Can Astor review my portfolio?


Yes, and you can start for free. Connect your accounts and ask whether you’re too concentrated, whether your funds overlap or whether your mix fits your timeline. Astor is an SEC-registered investment adviser, so its answers are personalized advice about what you own, and you make every decision.
